title: Free-Body Diagrams
short: Draw every force on one object as an arrow from its center, naming what exerts it.
trouble: Students draw a "force of motion" in the direction an object moves, or include forces the object exerts on other things.

blocks.html: You've met forces in Newton's Third Law and Friction. Before using Newton's laws on any problem, physicists draw a free-body diagram: one object, alone, with every force on it drawn as an arrow.

Draw the object as a box or a dot. For every force on it, draw an arrow from its center in the force's direction and name the object that exerts it. Contact forces come from things touching it; gravity comes from Earth.

Newton's laws relate the forces on one object to that object's motion. A diagram that leaves out a force, or adds one that isn't real, gives the wrong net force. Naming who exerts each force is the test: "the floor pushes up" is a real force; "the motion pushes forward" has no one doing the pushing, so it isn't a force.

blocks.name: ph-fbd

opts.task: Draw the forces on a box being pushed to the right across a rough floor at a steady speed, then check your diagram.

blocks.cap: Build the diagram: add each force from the list, drag its tip to set its size and direction, and check.

items: Earth's gravity: always, straight down, $F_g = mg$.
Each surface it touches: a normal force (perpendicular to the surface) and maybe friction (along the surface).
Each rope or string attached: a tension, pulling along the rope.
Anything else touching it: a push, a spring, the air.

blocks.title: A box pushed across a floor
blocks.q: You push a box across a rough floor at a steady speed. What forces act on it?
steps: Earth: gravity, down. The floor: a normal force, up, and kinetic friction, opposite to the sliding.
Your hand: the push, along its direction.
Four forces. At steady speed the push balances friction and the normal force balances gravity.
blocks.a: Gravity, normal force, friction and your push

blocks.title: A ball in flight
blocks.q: A ball flies up and to the right after you throw it. Ignoring air, what forces act on it?
steps: Nothing touches it, so there are no contact forces.
Only Earth's gravity, straight down. Your throw ended when the ball left your hand.

blocks.html: Drawing a "force of motion" in the direction the object moves, or including a force the object exerts on something else (like the box pushing on the floor). Moving objects keep moving on their own, so no force is needed to "carry" the motion; and forces the box exerts belong on the floor's diagram, not the box's. Check: for every arrow, finish the sentence "___ pushes or pulls on the box".
Try it in the Science Lab: Forces at Work builds diagrams for many everyday scenes.
